# Extension scaffold

Every file of the reference extension, the worked example that exercises each seam of the
protocol exactly once: a tool, a resource, its standing instructions, an HTTP route, a web
entry, a badge, and its own SQLite database. Copy it and delete what you do not need.

The reference extension is **standalone on purpose**. It has ordinary dependencies, its own
build, and belongs to no workspace, so everything below works the same in a repository of
your own.

## Starting from it

1. **Copy the folder** and rename it. `package.json` `name`, and the `name` in
   `src/server/manifest.ts`, are yours to change; the manifest name must be lowercase
   kebab-case.
2. **Install** with `pnpm install`. The `pnpm-workspace.yaml` in the folder is what keeps
   this local — it makes the directory a workspace root, so pnpm installs here rather than
   walking up to a parent workspace. Do not add `--ignore-workspace`: that skips the file,
   including the build allowance it carries, and the install fails.
3. **Build** with `pnpm build`. This writes `dist/`, which is what the host runs: the server
   entry and, if you keep the web entry, an ES module the client imports.
4. **Vendor the protocol types.** The reference extension keeps copies of
   `protocol.d.ts` and `protocol.schema.json` under `protocol/`; they are generated,
   dependency-free, and not reproduced here. Take them from the host repository's
   `packages/contracts/generated/extensions/`, or work from the JSON Schema alone if you are
   not writing TypeScript. Copy them again whenever you move to a newer protocol version —
   they are a snapshot, and nothing warns you when the host has moved on.

   The `sync:protocol` script you will see in `package.json` is how the in-tree reference
   extension does that same copy: it lives inside the host repository, so it can script it
   against a relative path and have a test fail when the copy falls behind. Outside the
   repository there is no such path, so drop the script — the copy is the part that matters,
   not how it is made.

5. **Point the host at it** with a settings entry naming the built folder, `dist/`. The host
   spawns the server entry on its own Node and passes everything it needs — name, token,
   WebSocket URL, data directory — as `T3_EXT_*` environment variables.

Nothing is inferred from the process: resolve your own files from `import.meta.url` rather
than `cwd`, treat the extension folder as read-only, and write only under the data directory
the host gives you.

## What is not here

The lockfile, the tests, the vendored protocol copies, and anything built. The tests are
worth reading in the host repository under `extensions/reference/test/` — they are what keeps
this scaffold honest.

### `pnpm-workspace.yaml`

```yaml
# This extension is standalone: it is deliberately NOT a member of the T3 Code
# repo's workspace (whose globs are apps/*, infra/*, packages/*, scripts — none
# of which match extensions/*). This file is what makes that true: its presence
# makes this directory a workspace root of its own, so a plain
# `pnpm install` here installs here.
#
# Do NOT pass --ignore-workspace. That flag skips this file, which also carries
# the esbuild build allowance below, and every install then ends in
# ERR_PNPM_IGNORED_BUILDS.
allowBuilds:
  esbuild: true
```

### `build.mjs`

```js
/**
 * The extension's own build. The host never watches source, installs, or
 * compiles: building is the extension's job, and the output folder is the unit
 * the host runs and content-hashes.
 *
 * Emits, per design §6.1:
 *   dist/extension.json  the manifest the host reads before spawning
 *   dist/server.mjs      one self-contained entry — every dependency bundled,
 *                        so the folder needs no node_modules and can sit in a
 *                        read-only app bundle
 *   dist/web/entry.js    an ES module exporting mount/unmount, own React
 *   dist/web/entry.css   scoped styles
 */
import * as esbuild from "esbuild";
import * as NodeChildProcess from "node:child_process";
import * as NodeModule from "node:module";
import * as NodeFSP from "node:fs/promises";
import * as NodePath from "node:path";
import * as NodeURL from "node:url";

const here = NodePath.dirname(NodeURL.fileURLToPath(import.meta.url));
const dist = NodePath.join(here, "dist");

await NodeFSP.rm(dist, { recursive: true, force: true });
await NodeFSP.mkdir(NodePath.join(dist, "web"), { recursive: true });

// The manifest is generated from the same module the server sends in
// `extensions.hello`, so dist/extension.json and the handshake cannot disagree.
const { MANIFEST } = await import("./src/server/manifest.ts");
await NodeFSP.writeFile(
  NodePath.join(dist, "extension.json"),
  `${JSON.stringify(MANIFEST, null, 2)}\n`,
);

// Node built-ins stay external in BOTH spellings. The `node:` prefix alone is
// not enough: a CommonJS dependency (ws) requires bare "events" and "http", and
// in ESM output esbuild turns an un-externalised require into a shim that
// throws "Dynamic require of \"events\" is not supported" at startup.
const nodeBuiltins = [
  ...NodeModule.builtinModules,
  ...NodeModule.builtinModules.map((name) => `node:${name}`),
];

await esbuild.build({
  entryPoints: [NodePath.join(here, "src/server/main.ts")],
  outfile: NodePath.join(dist, "server.mjs"),
  bundle: true,
  platform: "node",
  target: "node24",
  format: "esm",
  packages: "bundle",
  external: nodeBuiltins,
  // `ws` is CommonJS and requires bare built-ins ("events", "http", ...).
  // esbuild's ESM output emits a shim that defers to a global `require`, which
  // does not exist in a module — so the entry threw on import until this
  // banner supplied one. It only ever resolves built-ins; every non-builtin
  // dependency is still bundled, which the tests assert.
  banner: {
    js: [
      "#!/usr/bin/env node",
      'import { createRequire as __extensionCreateRequire } from "node:module";',
      "const require = __extensionCreateRequire(import.meta.url);",
    ].join("\n"),
  },
  logLevel: "info",
});

await esbuild.build({
  entryPoints: [NodePath.join(here, "src/web/entry.tsx")],
  outfile: NodePath.join(dist, "web/entry.js"),
  bundle: true,
  platform: "browser",
  target: "es2022",
  format: "esm",
  jsx: "automatic",
  // Production React, and `minify` never emits `eval` — but the CSP forbids
  // eval outright, so the check below verifies the output rather than trusting
  // the setting. `sourcemap: "external"` keeps eval-based sourcemaps out.
  define: { "process.env.NODE_ENV": '"production"' },
  minify: true,
  sourcemap: "external",
  logLevel: "info",
});

// The bundle is useless if it cannot run under the desktop CSP, and that
// failure would only show up at mount time in a packaged app. Fail the build
// instead.
const bundled = await NodeFSP.readFile(NodePath.join(dist, "web/entry.js"), "utf8");
const evalUse = /(?:^|[^.\w])eval\s*\(|new\s+Function\s*\(/.exec(bundled);
if (evalUse) {
  throw new Error(
    `Web bundle contains ${evalUse[0].trim()}, which the desktop CSP blocks ` +
      `(script-src has no 'unsafe-eval'). See docs/internals/extensions/spikes/electron-runtime.md.`,
  );
}

// A bundle that throws on import is the failure mode this build once shipped: a
// CommonJS dependency's `require` became a shim that threw at startup, and
// nothing noticed until the entry was run. Smoke-test it here.
//
// As a child process, not an `import`: the entry runs on load and exits, so
// importing it into the build would end the build.
const smoke = await new Promise((resolve) => {
  const child = NodeChildProcess.spawn(process.execPath, [NodePath.join(dist, "server.mjs")], {
    env: { PATH: process.env.PATH },
    stdio: ["ignore", "ignore", "pipe"],
  });
  let stderr = "";
  child.stderr.on("data", (chunk) => (stderr += chunk));
  child.on("exit", (code) => resolve({ code, stderr }));
});
// Exit 2 with the explanation is the entry correctly refusing to run without a
// host. Anything else means it did not get far enough to check.
if (smoke.code !== 2 || !/started by the host/.test(smoke.stderr)) {
  throw new Error(
    `Built server entry does not start (exit ${String(smoke.code)}):\n${smoke.stderr.trim()}`,
  );
}

console.log(`[build] wrote ${NodePath.relative(here, dist)}/`);
```

### `src/server/env.ts`

```ts
/**
 * The spawn contract: everything the host tells an extension at startup.
 *
 * These four variables are the entire interface between the host's supervisor
 * and the extension process. Nothing is read from `cwd` on purpose — a bundled
 * extension may live inside the packaged app's `app.asar`, and a path inside an
 * asar cannot be a process `cwd` (see spikes/electron-runtime.md), so an
 * extension that resolves its own files relative to `cwd` breaks when shipped.
 * Resolve from `import.meta.url` instead.
 */
/** The name the host registered this extension under; see `name` below. */
export const ENV_NAME = "T3_EXT_NAME";
export const ENV_TOKEN = "T3_EXT_TOKEN";
export const ENV_WS_URL = "T3_EXT_WS_URL";
export const ENV_DATA_DIR = "T3_EXT_DATA_DIR";
export const ENV_PROTOCOL_VERSION = "T3_EXT_PROTOCOL_VERSION";

export interface HostEnvironment {
  /**
   * The name the host knows this extension by.
   *
   * Authoritative over the manifest's own `name`: the same built folder can be
   * installed more than once, so the host decides which registration this
   * process is, and `extensions.connect` must use this rather than assume.
   */
  readonly name: string;
  readonly token: string;
  /** Absolute `ws://` or `wss://` URL, connected to verbatim. */
  readonly wsUrl: string;
  /** The per-environment directory this extension owns. It is the only place it may write. */
  readonly dataDirectory: string;
  readonly protocolVersion: number;
}

export class MissingHostEnvironmentError extends Error {
  constructor(readonly missing: ReadonlyArray<string>) {
    super(
      `This is a T3 Code extension: it is started by the host, not run directly.\n` +
        `Missing environment: ${missing.join(", ")}.\n` +
        `To run it by hand, set those variables to a host that is already listening.`,
    );
    this.name = "MissingHostEnvironmentError";
  }
}

/**
 * Reads the spawn contract, or explains precisely what is missing.
 *
 * Failing clearly here is what makes `node dist/server.mjs` a useful thing to
 * type: a human who runs the entry directly gets an explanation, not a stack
 * trace about an undefined URL.
 */
export function readHostEnvironment(source: NodeJS.ProcessEnv = process.env): HostEnvironment {
  const missing: string[] = [];
  const required = (name: string): string => {
    const value = source[name]?.trim();
    if (!value) missing.push(name);
    return value ?? "";
  };

  const name = required(ENV_NAME);
  const token = required(ENV_TOKEN);
  const wsUrl = required(ENV_WS_URL);
  const dataDirectory = required(ENV_DATA_DIR);
  const rawProtocolVersion = source[ENV_PROTOCOL_VERSION]?.trim();

  if (missing.length > 0) throw new MissingHostEnvironmentError(missing);

  // An absent protocol version means an older host; the manifest's version is
  // what we then negotiate with, and the host rejects it if it cannot speak it.
  const protocolVersion = rawProtocolVersion ? Number.parseInt(rawProtocolVersion, 10) : 1;
  if (!Number.isInteger(protocolVersion) || protocolVersion < 1) {
    throw new Error(
      `${ENV_PROTOCOL_VERSION} must be a positive integer, got "${rawProtocolVersion}".`,
    );
  }

  return { name, token, wsUrl, dataDirectory, protocolVersion };
}
```

### `src/server/http.ts`

```ts
/**
 * The extension's HTTP surface: a single `GET /status`.
 *
 * The host serves the registered prefix under its own origin and auth, then
 * proxies each request onto the stream. Two consequences worth knowing: remote,
 * relay, and tunnel clients reach this with no extra work, and the extension
 * never opens a port of its own.
 *
 * `path` arrives already stripped of the host's base path, so a route matches
 * against a plain "/status" regardless of where the host mounted the prefix.
 */
import type { ExtensionHttpRequest, ExtensionHttpResponse } from "../../protocol/protocol.js";
import type { EchoStore } from "./store.js";

export type HttpResponse = Omit<ExtensionHttpResponse, "connectionId">;

const json = (requestId: string, status: number, value: unknown): HttpResponse => ({
  requestId,
  status,
  headers: { "content-type": "application/json; charset=utf-8" },
  // Bodies are utf8 or base64 so binary survives a JSON wire.
  body: { encoding: "utf8", data: JSON.stringify(value) },
});

export function handleHttpRequest(
  store: EchoStore,
  startedAt: string,
  request: ExtensionHttpRequest,
): HttpResponse {
  const path = request.path.replace(/\/+$/, "") || "/";

  if (path === "/status" && (request.method === "GET" || request.method === "HEAD")) {
    const latest = store.latest();
    return json(request.requestId, 200, {
      name: "reference",
      startedAt,
      environmentId: request.environmentId,
      echoCount: store.count(),
      lastEcho: latest ?? null,
    });
  }

  return json(request.requestId, 404, { error: `No route for ${request.method} ${request.path}` });
}
```

### `src/server/main.ts`

```ts
/**
 * The reference extension's server entry.
 *
 * It exercises every seam in the protocol exactly once, in the order the host
 * expects: hello, then the declarative registrations, then `connect` last —
 * because opening the stream is the readiness signal, and the host may start
 * invoking tools the moment it exists.
 *
 * Read this file top to bottom to see the whole lifecycle of an extension.
 */
import type {
  ExtensionHelloAck,
  ExtensionHttpRequest,
  ExtensionManifest,
  ExtensionReadResourceRequest,
  ExtensionRegisterHttpPrefixResult,
  ExtensionRegisterResourcesResult,
  ExtensionRegisterToolsResult,
  ExtensionStreamEvent,
  ExtensionToolInvocation,
} from "../../protocol/protocol.js";
import { readHostEnvironment, MissingHostEnvironmentError } from "./env.js";
import { RpcClient, RpcConnectionClosedError } from "./rpc.js";
import { EchoStore } from "./store.js";
import { MANIFEST, HTTP_PREFIX, INSTRUCTIONS, RESOURCES, TOOLS, WEB_ENTRY } from "./manifest.js";
import { handleHttpRequest } from "./http.js";
import { readEchoResource } from "./resources.js";
import { runEchoTool } from "./tools.js";

/** Reconnect backoff. The host supervises the process; this only covers a socket blip. */
const RECONNECT_DELAY_MS = 1_000;

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  const env = readHostEnvironment();
  const store = new EchoStore(env.dataDirectory);
  const startedAt = new Date().toISOString();

  // The host holds registrations across a reconnect only for the connection
  // that made them, so a reconnect re-sends all of this verbatim. That is why
  // registration is idempotent and declarative rather than a diff.
  const session = async (): Promise<void> => {
    let reconnect = false;
    const client = await RpcClient.connect({
      url: env.wsUrl,
      token: env.token,
      onClose: (error: RpcConnectionClosedError) => {
        console.error(`[reference] host connection lost: ${error.message}`);
        reconnect = true;
      },
    });

    // 1. Handshake. The host answers with the negotiated version and our paths.
    // The host-assigned name overrides the manifest's own. The token's subject
    // is `extension:<name>`, and a token minted for one extension cannot say
    // hello as another — so the same built folder installed twice must
    // introduce itself as the installation it was spawned for, not as whatever
    // name it was built with. `extensions.connect` is verified against this.
    const manifest: ExtensionManifest = { ...MANIFEST, name: env.name };
    const ack = await client.call<ExtensionHelloAck>("extensions.hello", {
      protocolVersion: manifest.protocolVersion,
      manifest,
    });
    console.log(
      `[reference] connected to host ${ack.hostVersion} (protocol v${String(ack.protocolVersion)}), ` +
        // The directory this process actually writes to, which is the one the
        // host passed at spawn. In dev mode the operator chooses it, so it can
        // differ from the canonical path the host reports in the ack.
        `environment ${ack.environmentId}, data at ${env.dataDirectory}`,
    );

    // 2. Declarative registrations. Each is answered; a rejection is not fatal.
    // `instructions` rides with the tools because it is the same declaration:
    // what this extension is, and what its tools are for. The host appends it
    // to the MCP server's own instructions for every agent in the environment.
    const registered = await client.call<ExtensionRegisterToolsResult>("extensions.registerTools", {
      tools: TOOLS,
      instructions: INSTRUCTIONS,
    });
    for (const entry of registered.tools) {
      if (entry.status === "rejected") {
        // Losing a tool name is survivable: the rest of the extension still runs,
        // and Settings shows the reason. Do not exit.
        console.error(
          `[reference] tool "${entry.name}" rejected (${entry.reason}): ${entry.message}`,
        );
      }
    }

    // Resources are answered per URI, the same way tools are answered per name.
    const registeredResources = await client.call<ExtensionRegisterResourcesResult>(
      "extensions.registerResources",
      { resources: RESOURCES },
    );
    for (const entry of registeredResources.resources) {
      if (entry.status === "rejected") {
        console.error(
          `[reference] resource "${entry.uri}" rejected (${entry.reason}): ${entry.message}`,
        );
      }
    }

    const http = await client.call<ExtensionRegisterHttpPrefixResult>(
      "extensions.registerHttpPrefix",
      { prefix: HTTP_PREFIX },
    );
    console.log(`[reference] HTTP prefix "${http.prefix}" served at ${http.basePath}`);

    await client.call("extensions.registerWebEntry", { web: WEB_ENTRY });

    // The badge is host-held state: set it now so a reconnect restores the
    // count the user was already looking at.
    await client.call("extensions.setBadge", { badge: badgeFor(store.count()) });

    // 3. Open the stream last. This is the readiness signal.
    await new Promise<void>((resolve) => {
      let connectionId: string | undefined;

      client.stream(
        "extensions.connect",
        // The same name we said hello with; the host verifies the match.
        { name: manifest.name },
        (raw) => {
          const event = raw as ExtensionStreamEvent;
          switch (event.type) {
            case "attached":
              // A fresh id per connection: it is how the host drops an answer
              // that arrives from a process it has already given up on.
              connectionId = event.connectionId;
              console.log(`[reference] ready (connection ${event.connectionId})`);
              return;
            case "invokeTool":
              void respondToTool(client, store, connectionId, event.invocation);
              return;
            case "proxyHttp":
              void respondToHttp(client, store, connectionId, startedAt, event.request);
              return;
            case "readResource":
              void respondToReadResource(client, store, connectionId, event.request);
              return;
          }
        },
        (error) => {
          if (error) console.error(`[reference] stream ended: ${String(error)}`);
          resolve();
        },
      );
    });

    client.close();
    // The store deliberately outlives the socket: it is opened once for the
    // process and reused across reconnects. Closing it here and then recursing
    // would hand the next session a closed database.
    if (reconnect) {
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, RECONNECT_DELAY_MS));
      await session();
    }
  };

  try {
    await session();
  } finally {
    store.close();
  }
}

const badgeFor = (count: number) =>
  count === 0 ? ({ kind: "none" } as const) : ({ kind: "count", count } as const);

/**
 * Answers one `invokeTool`. Every failure is reported as a tool result with
 * `isError`, never as a thrown exception: the agent that called the tool should
 * read what went wrong, and the extension should stay up.
 */
async function respondToTool(
  client: RpcClient,
  store: EchoStore,
  connectionId: string | undefined,
  invocation: ExtensionToolInvocation,
): Promise<void> {
  if (!connectionId) return; // Nothing can be correlated before `attached`.
  try {
    const result = runEchoTool(store, invocation);
    await client.call("extensions.respondTool", { connectionId, ...result });
    // The badge tracks work this extension has actually done.
    await client.call("extensions.setBadge", { badge: badgeFor(store.count()) });
  } catch (error) {
    // Reporting the failure can itself fail if the socket just died. Swallow
    // that: the host already treats a missing answer as the extension being
    // unavailable, and an unhandled rejection here would take the process down.
    await client
      .call("extensions.respondTool", {
        connectionId,
        invocationId: invocation.invocationId,
        content: [{ type: "text", text: `Reference extension failed: ${String(error)}` }],
        isError: true,
      })
      .catch(() => undefined);
  }
}

/**
 * Answers one `readResource`. There is no `isError` shape for a resource, so a
 * failure has to be a *missing* answer: the host times the call out and turns
 * it into an MCP protocol error carrying its own sentence. Nothing useful can
 * be sent back here, which is why this only logs.
 */
async function respondToReadResource(
  client: RpcClient,
  store: EchoStore,
  connectionId: string | undefined,
  request: ExtensionReadResourceRequest,
): Promise<void> {
  if (!connectionId) return;
  try {
    const result = readEchoResource(store, request);
    await client.call("extensions.respondReadResource", { connectionId, ...result });
  } catch (error) {
    console.error(`[reference] failed to read ${request.uri}: ${String(error)}`);
  }
}

/** Answers one `proxyHttp`. Same rule: an error is a 500 response, not a crash. */
async function respondToHttp(
  client: RpcClient,
  store: EchoStore,
  connectionId: string | undefined,
  startedAt: string,
  request: ExtensionHttpRequest,
): Promise<void> {
  if (!connectionId) return;
  try {
    const response = handleHttpRequest(store, startedAt, request);
    await client.call("extensions.respondHttp", { connectionId, ...response });
  } catch (error) {
    await client
      .call("extensions.respondHttp", {
        connectionId,
        requestId: request.requestId,
        status: 500,
        headers: { "content-type": "text/plain; charset=utf-8" },
        body: { encoding: "utf8", data: `Reference extension failed: ${String(error)}` },
      })
      .catch(() => undefined);
  }
}

main().catch((error: unknown) => {
  // A missing spawn contract is a human running the entry by hand: explain it
  // without a stack trace. Anything else is a real fault worth the full trace.
  if (error instanceof MissingHostEnvironmentError) {
    console.error(error.message);
    process.exit(2);
  }
  console.error(error);
  process.exit(1);
});
```

### `src/server/manifest.ts`

```ts
/**
 * The extension's declared surface, in one place.
 *
 * `MANIFEST` is also what the build writes to `dist/extension.json`, so the
 * file the host reads before spawning and the value sent in `extensions.hello`
 * can never disagree.
 */
import type {
  ExtensionHttpPrefix,
  ExtensionManifest,
  ExtensionResourceDefinition,
  ExtensionToolDefinition,
  ExtensionWebEntry,
} from "../../protocol/protocol.js";

/** Unprefixed and unique across the environment; a collision is rejected by name. */
export const ECHO_TOOL_NAME = "reference_echo";

export const HTTP_PREFIX: ExtensionHttpPrefix = "reference";

export const TOOLS: ReadonlyArray<ExtensionToolDefinition> = [
  {
    name: ECHO_TOOL_NAME,
    description:
      "Echoes its arguments back, together with the caller identity the host attached. " +
      "Demonstrates that an extension never has to trust the agent for who is calling.",
    inputSchema: {
      type: "object",
      properties: {
        message: { type: "string", description: "Text to echo back." },
      },
      required: ["message"],
      additionalProperties: false,
    },
  },
];

/** Unique across the environment, like a tool name; the host's own `t3code://` URIs are taken. */
export const ECHO_RESOURCE_URI = "reference://echoes";

export const RESOURCES: ReadonlyArray<ExtensionResourceDefinition> = [
  {
    uri: ECHO_RESOURCE_URI,
    name: "reference-echoes",
    description:
      "Everything reference_echo has recorded, newest first. Read it to see what an " +
      "extension-owned resource looks like: the host lists it beside its own and forwards " +
      "the read here.",
    mimeType: "application/json",
  },
];

/**
 * Standing guidance for every agent in the environment, appended to the MCP
 * server's own instructions.
 *
 * Kept to a few sentences on purpose. It is billed on every turn of every
 * thread and the whole server-level string is shared with the host's own
 * paragraph and with any other extension, so an extension that writes a page
 * here is an extension that pushes the next one out. What belongs here is what
 * an agent cannot work out from a tool description: what this extension *is*,
 * and when not to reach for it.
 */
export const INSTRUCTIONS = [
  "The `reference` extension is a worked example of the extension protocol, not a working tool.",
  `Its \`${ECHO_TOOL_NAME}\` tool echoes a message back with the caller identity the host resolved,`,
  `and \`${ECHO_RESOURCE_URI}\` lists what it has recorded.`,
  "Neither changes anything in a project, so do not reach for them to get work done.",
].join(" ");

export const WEB_ENTRY: ExtensionWebEntry = {
  entry: "web/entry.js",
  css: "web/entry.css",
  label: "Reference",
};

export const MANIFEST: ExtensionManifest = {
  name: "reference",
  version: "1.0.0",
  protocolVersion: 1,
  server: { entry: "server.mjs" },
  web: WEB_ENTRY,
};
```

### `src/server/resources.ts`

```ts
/**
 * The one resource this extension registers.
 *
 * A resource is the read-only half of what an extension contributes to MCP:
 * the host lists it beside its own `t3code://` resources and forwards each
 * `resources/read` here over the stream. Unlike a tool invocation it carries
 * **no caller** — MCP reads a resource by URI and tells the server nothing
 * about who asked — so anything that has to be scoped to a thread belongs in a
 * tool, which does get `invocation.caller`.
 *
 * The other asymmetry worth knowing: there is no `isError` result. A read that
 * cannot be answered has to go unanswered, and the host turns that into an MCP
 * protocol error. So answer with whatever is true — an empty list is a real
 * answer — and save failing for an actual failure.
 *
 * The answer quotes the URI it was asked for rather than a constant of its
 * own. The host routes by URI and only ever sends one this extension
 * registered, so re-deriving it here would only be a second place to keep in
 * step with the manifest.
 */
import type {
  ExtensionReadResourceRequest,
  ExtensionReadResourceResult,
} from "../../protocol/protocol.js";
import type { EchoStore } from "./store.js";

export type ReadResourceResult = Omit<ExtensionReadResourceResult, "connectionId">;

export function readEchoResource(
  store: EchoStore,
  request: ExtensionReadResourceRequest,
): ReadResourceResult {
  const latest = store.latest();
  return {
    requestId: request.requestId,
    contents: [
      {
        type: "text",
        uri: request.uri,
        mimeType: "application/json",
        text: JSON.stringify({ echoCount: store.count(), lastEcho: latest ?? null }, null, 2),
      },
    ],
  };
}
```

### `src/server/rpc.ts`

```ts
/**
 * A minimal client for the host's RPC-over-WebSocket protocol.
 *
 * The host serves Effect RPC with `RpcSerialization.layerJson`
 * (`apps/server/src/ws.ts`), which means: one JSON value per WebSocket frame,
 * and a frame may be either a single message or an array of them. This file is
 * the whole wire contract an extension needs — deliberately hand-written with
 * no Effect dependency, because an extension is a separate process that may be
 * written in any language and must not need the host's toolchain.
 *
 * Client -> host frames:
 *   {"_tag":"Request","id":<n>,"tag":"<method>","payload":<value>,"headers":[]}
 *   {"_tag":"Ack","requestId":<n>}          // request one more chunk of a stream
 *   {"_tag":"Interrupt","requestId":<n>}    // cancel a request or stream
 *   {"_tag":"Ping"}
 *
 * Host -> client frames:
 *   {"_tag":"Exit","requestId":<n>,"exit":{"_tag":"Success","value":<v>}}
 *   {"_tag":"Exit","requestId":<n>,"exit":{"_tag":"Failure","cause":[...]}}
 *   {"_tag":"Chunk","requestId":<n>,"values":[<v>, ...]}   // one stream batch
 *   {"_tag":"Defect","defect":<v>} | {"_tag":"Pong"} | {"_tag":"ClientProtocolError","error":<v>}
 *
 * Streams are pull-based: the host sends a `Chunk` only after the client has
 * acknowledged the previous one. Forgetting the `Ack` is the classic way to
 * make a stream look dead after exactly one event.
 */
import { WebSocket } from "ws";

export type RpcRequestId = number;

/** A `Failure` exit turned into a throwable, keeping the host's typed error intact. */
export class RpcCallError extends Error {
  constructor(
    readonly method: string,
    readonly cause: unknown,
  ) {
    super(`${method} failed: ${JSON.stringify(cause)}`);
    this.name = "RpcCallError";
  }
}

export class RpcConnectionClosedError extends Error {
  constructor(readonly code?: number) {
    super(`Host connection closed${code === undefined ? "" : ` (code ${String(code)})`}.`);
    this.name = "RpcConnectionClosedError";
  }
}

interface PendingCall {
  readonly method: string;
  readonly resolve: (value: unknown) => void;
  readonly reject: (error: unknown) => void;
}

interface StreamSubscription {
  readonly onValue: (value: unknown) => void;
  readonly onEnd: (error: unknown) => void;
}

export interface RpcClientOptions {
  readonly url: string;
  readonly token: string;
  /** Called for every stream/connection failure; the caller decides whether to retry. */
  readonly onClose: (error: RpcConnectionClosedError) => void;
}

export class RpcClient {
  #socket: WebSocket;
  #nextId: RpcRequestId = 1;
  #calls = new Map<RpcRequestId, PendingCall>();
  #streams = new Map<RpcRequestId, StreamSubscription>();
  #closed = false;

  private constructor(
    socket: WebSocket,
    private readonly onClose: RpcClientOptions["onClose"],
  ) {
    this.#socket = socket;
    socket.on("message", (raw: Buffer | string) => this.#receive(raw.toString()));
    socket.on("close", (code: number) => this.#fail(new RpcConnectionClosedError(code)));
    socket.on("error", (error: Error) => this.#fail(error));
  }

  /**
   * The token rides as an `Authorization` header on the handshake. Browsers
   * cannot set handshake headers and use the host's ticket query parameter
   * instead; a spawned extension is not a browser, so it takes the simpler path.
   */
  static connect(options: RpcClientOptions): Promise<RpcClient> {
    return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      const socket = new WebSocket(options.url, {
        headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${options.token}` },
      });
      const onError = (error: Error) => reject(error);
      socket.once("error", onError);
      socket.once("open", () => {
        socket.off("error", onError);
        resolve(new RpcClient(socket, options.onClose));
      });
    });
  }

  /** One request, one `Exit`. Rejects with `RpcCallError` on a typed failure. */
  call<Result>(method: string, payload: unknown): Promise<Result> {
    return new Promise<Result>((resolve, reject) => {
      if (this.#closed) return reject(new RpcConnectionClosedError());
      const id = this.#nextId++;
      this.#calls.set(id, { method, resolve: resolve as (value: unknown) => void, reject });
      this.#send({ _tag: "Request", id, tag: method, payload, headers: [] });
    });
  }

  /**
   * Subscribes to a streaming method. Returns the request id so the caller can
   * `interrupt` it. Each delivered value is acknowledged immediately, which is
   * what keeps the host sending.
   */
  stream(
    method: string,
    payload: unknown,
    onValue: (value: unknown) => void,
    onEnd: (error: unknown) => void,
  ): RpcRequestId {
    const id = this.#nextId++;
    this.#streams.set(id, { onValue, onEnd });
    this.#send({ _tag: "Request", id, tag: method, payload, headers: [] });
    return id;
  }

  interrupt(requestId: RpcRequestId): void {
    this.#streams.delete(requestId);
    this.#send({ _tag: "Interrupt", requestId });
  }

  close(): void {
    this.#closed = true;
    this.#socket.close();
  }

  #send(message: unknown): void {
    if (this.#socket.readyState === WebSocket.OPEN) {
      this.#socket.send(JSON.stringify(message));
    }
  }

  #receive(raw: string): void {
    let parsed: unknown;
    try {
      parsed = JSON.parse(raw);
    } catch {
      return; // A frame we cannot parse is the host's problem, not a reason to die.
    }
    for (const message of Array.isArray(parsed) ? parsed : [parsed]) {
      this.#handle(message as Record<string, unknown>);
    }
  }

  #handle(message: Record<string, unknown>): void {
    switch (message._tag) {
      case "Exit": {
        const id = message.requestId as RpcRequestId;
        const exit = message.exit as { _tag: string; value?: unknown; cause?: unknown };
        const call = this.#calls.get(id);
        if (call) {
          this.#calls.delete(id);
          if (exit._tag === "Success") call.resolve(exit.value);
          else call.reject(new RpcCallError(call.method, exit.cause));
          return;
        }
        // A stream's Exit is its end: clean for Success, an error otherwise.
        const stream = this.#streams.get(id);
        if (stream) {
          this.#streams.delete(id);
          stream.onEnd(
            exit._tag === "Success" ? undefined : new RpcCallError("stream", exit.cause),
          );
        }
        return;
      }
      case "Chunk": {
        const id = message.requestId as RpcRequestId;
        const stream = this.#streams.get(id);
        if (!stream) return;
        for (const value of message.values as ReadonlyArray<unknown>) stream.onValue(value);
        // Pull the next batch. Without this the stream stalls after one chunk.
        this.#send({ _tag: "Ack", requestId: id });
        return;
      }
      case "Ping":
        this.#send({ _tag: "Pong" });
        return;
      default:
        return; // Pong, Defect, ClientProtocolError: nothing useful to do here.
    }
  }

  #fail(error: unknown): void {
    const closed =
      error instanceof RpcConnectionClosedError ? error : new RpcConnectionClosedError();
    for (const [, call] of this.#calls) call.reject(closed);
    this.#calls.clear();
    for (const [, stream] of this.#streams) stream.onEnd(closed);
    this.#streams.clear();
    if (!this.#closed) {
      this.#closed = true;
      this.onClose(closed);
    }
  }
}
```

### `src/server/store.ts`

```ts
/**
 * The extension's own database.
 *
 * `node:sqlite` is built into Node 24 and into the Node that Electron 43 ships,
 * so an extension needs no native dependency to persist anything (verified in
 * spikes/electron-runtime.md). The file lives in the host-assigned data
 * directory: the extension folder itself is read-only when shipped inside an
 * app bundle.
 *
 * The extension owns this schema outright. The host adds no tables and runs no
 * migrations here — which is what lets the fork share a T3 home with upstream.
 */
import * as NodeSqlite from "node:sqlite";
import * as NodeFS from "node:fs";
import * as NodePath from "node:path";

export interface EchoRecord {
  readonly id: number;
  readonly at: string;
  readonly threadId: string;
  readonly message: string;
}

export class EchoStore {
  #db: NodeSqlite.DatabaseSync;

  constructor(dataDirectory: string) {
    NodeFS.mkdirSync(dataDirectory, { recursive: true });
    this.#db = new NodeSqlite.DatabaseSync(
      NodePath.join(dataDirectory, "reference-extension.sqlite"),
    );
    // Migrations are the extension's job, run at its own cadence on startup.
    this.#db.exec(`
      CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS echoes (
        id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
        at TEXT NOT NULL,
        thread_id TEXT NOT NULL,
        message TEXT NOT NULL
      )
    `);
  }

  record(threadId: string, message: string): EchoRecord {
    const at = new Date().toISOString();
    const { lastInsertRowid } = this.#db
      .prepare("INSERT INTO echoes (at, thread_id, message) VALUES (?, ?, ?)")
      .run(at, threadId, message);
    return { id: Number(lastInsertRowid), at, threadId, message };
  }

  count(): number {
    const row = this.#db.prepare("SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM echoes").get() as { n: number };
    return row.n;
  }

  latest(): EchoRecord | undefined {
    const row = this.#db
      .prepare("SELECT id, at, thread_id AS threadId, message FROM echoes ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1")
      .get() as EchoRecord | undefined;
    return row;
  }

  close(): void {
    this.#db.close();
  }
}
```

### `src/server/tools.ts`

```ts
/**
 * The one tool this extension registers.
 *
 * The interesting part is `invocation.caller`: the host resolves the thread,
 * environment, and provider instance itself and attaches them to every
 * invocation. An agent cannot claim to be someone else by writing it into the
 * arguments, so an extension can use the caller identity for authorization
 * without validating anything.
 */
import type { ExtensionToolInvocation, ExtensionToolResult } from "../../protocol/protocol.js";
import type { EchoStore } from "./store.js";

export type EchoToolResult = Omit<ExtensionToolResult, "connectionId">;

export function runEchoTool(store: EchoStore, invocation: ExtensionToolInvocation): EchoToolResult {
  const message =
    typeof invocation.arguments.message === "string" ? invocation.arguments.message : "";
  if (message.length === 0) {
    // A bad argument is a tool error the agent can read and correct, not an
    // exception: the extension stays up and the agent gets a usable message.
    return {
      invocationId: invocation.invocationId,
      content: [{ type: "text", text: 'reference_echo requires a non-empty string "message".' }],
      isError: true,
    };
  }

  const record = store.record(invocation.caller.threadId, message);

  return {
    invocationId: invocation.invocationId,
    content: [
      {
        type: "text",
        text: `Echo #${String(record.id)}: ${message}\nCalled from thread ${invocation.caller.threadId} on ${invocation.caller.providerInstanceId}.`,
      },
    ],
    // Structured content is what a caller should parse; the text above is for
    // the agent to read.
    structuredContent: {
      echoId: record.id,
      message: record.message,
      at: record.at,
      caller: invocation.caller,
      totalEchoes: store.count(),
    },
  };
}
```

### `src/web/App.tsx`

```tsx
/**
 * The extension's UI: current status and the last echo.
 *
 * Every class name is prefixed `t3ref-`, and the stylesheet sets no element
 * selectors at all. An extension's CSS lands in the host's document, so a
 * Tailwind preflight or a bare `button { }` here would restyle the host.
 */
import { useCallback, useEffect, useState } from "react";
import type { HostApi, StatusPayload } from "./hostApi.js";

interface AppProps {
  readonly hostApi: HostApi;
  readonly subPath: string;
}

export function App({ hostApi, subPath }: AppProps) {
  const [status, setStatus] = useState<StatusPayload | null>(null);
  const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);

  const refresh = useCallback(async () => {
    setLoading(true);
    try {
      // Relative to the prefix the host mounted for us; the host's authenticated
      // fetch supplies origin and credentials.
      const response = await hostApi.fetch(hostApi.environmentId, "/status");
      if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Host returned ${String(response.status)}`);
      setStatus((await response.json()) as StatusPayload);
      setError(null);
    } catch (cause) {
      setError(cause instanceof Error ? cause.message : String(cause));
    } finally {
      setLoading(false);
    }
  }, [hostApi]);

  useEffect(() => {
    void refresh();
  }, [refresh]);

  return (
    <div className="t3ref-root">
      <header className="t3ref-header">
        <h1 className="t3ref-title">Reference extension</h1>
        <button className="t3ref-button" onClick={() => void refresh()} disabled={loading}>
          {loading ? "Refreshing…" : "Refresh"}
        </button>
      </header>

      {/* Colors come from the host's CSS variables, so the extension follows
          the user's theme without knowing which theme is active. */}
      {error !== null && <p className="t3ref-error">Could not reach the extension: {error}</p>}

      {status !== null && (
        <dl className="t3ref-grid">
          <dt className="t3ref-key">Environment</dt>
          <dd className="t3ref-value">{status.environmentId}</dd>
          <dt className="t3ref-key">Started</dt>
          <dd className="t3ref-value">{new Date(status.startedAt).toLocaleString()}</dd>
          <dt className="t3ref-key">Echoes</dt>
          <dd className="t3ref-value">{status.echoCount}</dd>
          <dt className="t3ref-key">Last echo</dt>
          <dd className="t3ref-value">
            {status.lastEcho === null ? (
              <span className="t3ref-muted">
                None yet — ask an agent to call <code className="t3ref-code">reference_echo</code>.
              </span>
            ) : (
              <>
                <span className="t3ref-echo">{status.lastEcho.message}</span>{" "}
                <button
                  className="t3ref-link"
                  onClick={() => hostApi.navigateToThread(status.lastEcho!.threadId)}
                >
                  open thread
                </button>
              </>
            )}
          </dd>
        </dl>
      )}

      {subPath !== "" && subPath !== "/" && (
        <p className="t3ref-muted">
          Sub-path <code className="t3ref-code">{subPath}</code> — the host owns
          <code className="t3ref-code"> /ext/&lt;env&gt;/reference/*</code> and hands the rest here.
        </p>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}
```

### `src/web/entry.tsx`

```tsx
/**
 * The web entry: the ES module the host `import()`s and mounts.
 *
 * The host loads this with a same-origin dynamic `import()`, the only strategy
 * that executes under the desktop's Content-Security-Policy (see
 * spikes/electron-runtime.md). Two constraints follow, and both are enforced by
 * the build rather than by hoping:
 *
 *   - No `eval` and no `new Function`. `script-src` carries no 'unsafe-eval',
 *     so any bundler mode that emits `eval()` — webpack's `eval-source-map`,
 *     dev-mode HMR wrappers — produces a bundle that cannot run at all.
 *   - No `blob:` or `data:` URLs for further code loading. Static and dynamic
 *     `import()` of same-origin paths is the only route in.
 *
 * This module brings its own React. Two Reacts on one page are only a problem
 * when one renders components from the other's tree, which never happens here:
 * the host hands over a plain DOM container and this owns everything inside it.
 */
import { StrictMode } from "react";
import { createRoot, type Root } from "react-dom/client";

// Bundled by the build into a sibling entry.css, which the manifest declares
// and the host injects. Kept out of the JS so no style is applied by script.
import "./styles.css";

import { App } from "./App.js";
import type { HostApi } from "./hostApi.js";

/**
 * Roots keyed by container, not by a module-level singleton.
 *
 * The same extension can be mounted twice in one page under two different
 * environments, so nothing here may be keyed by extension name or held in a
 * module-scope variable that assumes a single instance.
 */
const roots = new WeakMap<Element, Root>();

/** Called by the host to mount the extension into a container it owns. */
export function mount(container: Element, hostApi: HostApi, subPath: string): void {
  const existing = roots.get(container);
  const root = existing ?? createRoot(container);
  if (!existing) roots.set(container, root);
  root.render(
    <StrictMode>
      <App hostApi={hostApi} subPath={subPath} />
    </StrictMode>,
  );
}

/**
 * Called by the host before it discards the container.
 *
 * Unmounting is what makes navigating away and back cheap, and what stops a
 * pending fetch from calling setState on a torn-down tree.
 */
export function unmount(container: Element): void {
  const root = roots.get(container);
  if (!root) return;
  roots.delete(container);
  root.unmount();
}
```

### `src/web/hostApi.ts`

```ts
/**
 * The slice of the host's web API this extension uses.
 *
 * Typed here rather than imported: the web bundle is standalone too, and
 * importing host types would be a workspace link through the back door.
 */
export interface HostEnvironment {
  readonly environmentId: string;
  readonly label: string;
  readonly current: boolean;
}

export interface HostApi {
  /** The environment this mount belongs to; the usual argument to `fetch`. */
  readonly environmentId: string;
  /**
   * Authenticated request to this extension's own HTTP prefix on one
   * environment. Naming the environment is what lets a mount reach the sibling
   * instance running on another one; for its own, pass `hostApi.environmentId`.
   */
  readonly fetch: (environmentId: string, path: string, init?: RequestInit) => Promise<Response>;
  readonly environments: ReadonlyArray<HostEnvironment>;
  readonly navigateToThread: (threadId: string, environmentId?: string) => void;
}

export interface StatusPayload {
  readonly name: string;
  readonly startedAt: string;
  readonly environmentId: string;
  readonly echoCount: number;
  readonly lastEcho: {
    readonly id: number;
    readonly at: string;
    readonly threadId: string;
    readonly message: string;
  } | null;
}
```

```css
/* Every rule is scoped to a `t3ref-` class. No element or `:root` selectors:
   this stylesheet is injected into the host's document, so an unscoped rule
   would restyle the whole app. Colors read the host's theme variables, with
   fallbacks so the bundle still looks right if a variable is renamed. */
.t3ref-root {
  padding: 24px;
  color: var(--color-foreground, #262626);
  font-family: inherit;
}
.t3ref-header {
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: space-between;

}
```
